newsitem.title: USA: Ohio task force unveils $5.8 bln plan for schools.
newsitem.headline: Ohio task force unveils $5.8 bln plan for schools.

text.p: Ohio's task force for school funding reforms recommended Tuesday that the state provide $5.8 billion for a matching capital improvements program over the next 10 years.

The task force also recommended raising the state sales tax one percent, the cigarette tax by 12 cents per pack and reducing a business property tax rollback to partly fund $1.1 billion for state aid to schools for the current fiscal biennium.

Ohio Supreme Court justices in March overturned the state's school funding mechanisms in a narrow 4-3 decision. The Court gave Ohio one year to revamp its funding policies and Gov. George Voinovich appointed the task force shortly thereafter.

The task force report prepared by Chairman Greg Browning suggested that the state aid for building could leverage about $7 billion in local funds for capital improvements in the fiscal 1998 to 2007 period as well.
The final plans for funding reforms will include a series of constitutional amendments to be submitted to voters in November, Voinovich said in a statement.

"I've said from the very beginning that people will support the idea of providing more money for education, but they want to see results -- they want to make sure they're getting a return on their investment," Voinovich said.

The building program would be financed by raising the state sales tax and reserving a portion of the increase for facilities while at the same time limiting funding for other improvements to inflationary increases during the next two capital budgets, the report found.

The recommended $1.1 billion increase for the current fiscal biennium would be an addition to the $600 million increase for elementary and secondary education included in the budget signed by Voinovich Monday.
The sales tax increase would generate about $1.1 billion annually, while the cigarette tax hike would raise about $102 million per year and the business property tax increase about $103 million.

The plan would give local school districts more opportunity to levy property taxes to meet their local contribution to state aid with voter approval. The districts would also be allowed to propose levies exempt from reduction and for limited growth levies at a specified fixed percentage.
The plan would also provide some property tax reductions for homeowners and create a deduction for primary and secondary educational expenses.
